name: Precision hold
description: Lining up one deliberate shot. For example scout rifles, linear fusion rifles and bows.

favours.text: Fine control at low speed without losing turn speed. The line-up is slow, fine aim (Precision). Getting there is fast aim (Response). A custom aiming curve can make slow movements finer while keeping full speed at the top. The smoothing directions (Precision, Response, Easing and, for motion aim, Stability) assume custom Standard smoothing (your own values, not a preset): it adapts to your current aim speed, so slow and fast aim can be tuned apart. Classic smoothing is static (it doesn't adapt to your aim speed), so Classic users get the definitions but not those directions. The aiming curve is a separate setting from smoothing, so this doesn't apply to it.

citations.quote: Controls fine aim behavior
Controls fast aim behavior
The Standard system provides dynamic smoothing behavior that adapts to your current aim speed.
The Classic system is based on our past generation XIM APEX device which provides static smoothing behavior.
A curve represents how your reticle speed transitions from 0 to 100% velocity (bottom left of the curve to upper right).

favours.reasoning: A deliberate shot is usually a fast move to the target area, then a slow line-up. Precision "controls fine aim behavior" and Response "controls fast aim behavior". An aiming curve maps reticle speed "from 0 to 100% velocity", so a curve that stays below the straight line at low speed but still reaches full speed at the top makes slow aim finer without lowering the top speed. Standard "adapts to your current aim speed", which is what lets a setting target one speed range without changing the others. Classic "provides static smoothing behavior", so the speed-based directions don't carry over. XIM's guide doesn't tie any setting to an aim style. XIM Central's 2023 tutorials for other games do in places. For Overwatch 2, XIM Central says a custom smoothing setup and an aiming curve help with flicks, both tied to that game's aim assist. For Rainbow Six Siege, XIM Central says the Light smoothing preset helps with micro aiming. Neither tutorial is about Destiny 2, so these directions rest on XIM's definitions.

statement.text: Precision shapes the slow line-up, and it cuts both ways. Raise it if the line-up shakes. Lower it if the line-up feels heavy or sluggish. XIM's definition gives the trade-off: a smoother result at low speed, but a heavier reticle.

citations.quote: Controls fine aim behavior
Higher values provide a smoother result at low aim speeds and increases the heaviness of the reticle.
Both mouse and motion have different presets designed for those aiming methods. Start by trying each out to see what feels most natural to you. It's strictly based on preference.
You can also customize the smoothing system and choose between two smoothing modes: Standard and Classic.

statement.reasoning: A deliberate line-up is slow, fine movement, which Precision controls. Higher values give "a smoother result at low aim speeds" and "increases the heaviness of the reticle". Which way helps depends on whether your problem is shake or weight.
statement.caveat: Assumes custom Standard smoothing (Precision is a Standard setting; Classic uses Smooth, Decay and Synch instead). If you use a smoothing preset, XIM suggests trying the other presets first.

statement.text: Response shapes the fast move onto the target. If that move feels heavy, raise Response. If it feels too light, lower it.

citations.quote: Controls fast aim behavior
Higher values produces a lighter feeling reticle at faster aim speeds.
Both mouse and motion have different presets designed for those aiming methods. Start by trying each out to see what feels most natural to you. It's strictly based on preference.
You can also customize the smoothing system and choose between two smoothing modes: Standard and Classic.

statement.reasoning: The move to the target area is fast aim, which Response "controls". Higher values produce "a lighter feeling reticle at faster aim speeds". The definition only says which way is lighter; which way you need depends on your feel.
statement.caveat: Assumes custom Standard smoothing (Response is a Standard setting). If you use a smoothing preset, XIM suggests trying the other presets first.

statement.text: Easing shapes how the line-up starts from a standstill. If that start jerks, raise Easing for a smoother start. If it feels slow to get going, lower it.

citations.quote: Specifies aim behavior from rest
Higher values result in smoother transition from rest but lower response time.
Both mouse and motion have different presets designed for those aiming methods. Start by trying each out to see what feels most natural to you. It's strictly based on preference.
You can also customize the smoothing system and choose between two smoothing modes: Standard and Classic.

statement.reasoning: A careful line-up often starts with the reticle at rest, and Easing "specifies aim behavior from rest". Higher values give a "smoother transition from rest but lower response time". We read that as a smoother but slower start. Which way helps depends on whether your start jerks or drags.
statement.caveat: The official wording is ambiguous: we read 'lower response time' as less responsive because of the 'but'. Confirm in-game before relying on it. Assumes custom Standard smoothing (Easing is a Standard setting). If you use a smoothing preset, XIM suggests trying the other presets first.

statement.text: A custom aiming curve can give finer control on the slow line-up while keeping full speed for the move onto the target. One example: a curve that sits below the straight line at low speed but still reaches full speed at the top. The cost: your cm/360 no longer matches physically.

citations.quote: A curve represents how your reticle speed transitions from 0 to 100% velocity (bottom left of the curve to upper right).
You can craft any curve you want: such as a simple acceleration curve or a more complex multiple zone curves. Presets are included for more common curves.
In the linear case, speed in produces the same exact speed out. The default curve is linear (a straight diagonal line).
An accurate cm/360 means that your mouse behavior physically matches your sensitivity setting when using a linear (default) aim response curve.
Do not use any aiming curves other than the default linear.

statement.reasoning: A curve maps input speed to reticle speed from 0 to 100%, and the default linear curve is one-to-one. Outputting less than linear at low input speed makes slow movements finer. Still reaching 100% keeps the top speed. The guide names curve types (a simple acceleration curve, or more complex multiple zone curves) and says presets are included for more common curves, but it recommends no custom shape, and cm/360 is only exact with a linear curve.
statement.caveat: Whether a curve helps depends on its shape and on your feel; the guide recommends none. Use a linear curve when you check your cm/360. XIM's SAB checklist says not to use aiming curves.

statement.text: Motion (gyro) aim only: if the reticle wobbles while you hold still on the spot, raise Stability. It adds steadiness at rest.

citations.quote: Specifies aim behavior at rest
Increase to provide extra stability at rest due to hand jitter and instability (motion aim only).
Both mouse and motion have different presets designed for those aiming methods. Start by trying each out to see what feels most natural to you. It's strictly based on preference.
You can also customize the smoothing system and choose between two smoothing modes: Standard and Classic.

statement.reasoning: A deliberate shot often means holding still on a spot, which is aim at rest. Stability "specifies aim behavior at rest", and raising it gives "extra stability at rest". No source ties it to aim styles.
statement.caveat: Motion aim only. Assumes custom Standard smoothing (Stability is a Standard setting). If you use a smoothing preset, XIM suggests trying the other presets first.

mapping.text: Scout rifles are precision-hold weapons: you line up one deliberate shot at a time, usually at long range.
mapping.reasoning: Most scout rifles fire one shot per trigger pull and reward hitting the head at range. Each shot is aimed on its own, and at long range a target moves only a little on screen. So the skill is fine control at low aim speed to settle the reticle exactly, which is precision hold.
mapping.caveat: Based on how this weapon type fires, not on a source: no whitelisted source covers Destiny 2 weapons. Loose fit: some scout rifles fire full auto while you hold the trigger (Rapid-Fire Frame scouts, some Exotics such as Symmetry, and any scout with the Full Auto Trigger System perk). Staying on target through that stream of shots is closer to tracking.

mapping.text: Combat bows are precision-hold weapons: you line up one shot and fire it deliberately.
mapping.reasoning: A drawn bow fires one arrow per draw, and the draw gives you time to settle the reticle before you release. A precision hit matters. So the skill is fine control at low aim speed on a single shot, which is precision hold.
mapping.caveat: Based on how this weapon type fires, not on a source: no whitelisted source covers Destiny 2 weapons. Crossbows also count as Combat Bows in the game: the Heavy-ammo crossbows in the Power slot, and the Exotic Heirloom in the Energy slot (Special ammo). They are not drawn: they fire bolts and have a Rounds Per Minute stat instead of a Draw Time, so the draw part of this reasoning does not apply to them.

mapping.text: Grenade launchers are closest to precision-hold weapons: you place single explosive shots at the right spot, often a target's feet.
mapping.reasoning: A grenade usually travels in an arc and explodes on impact or nearby. The skill is placing each shot at the right spot, not holding on a target or flicking to a head. That is closest to lining up a single deliberate shot.
mapping.caveat: Based on how this weapon type fires, not on a source: no whitelisted source covers Destiny 2 weapons. Loose fit: splash damage makes exact aim matter less than with other weapons.

mapping.text: Linear fusion rifles are precision-hold weapons: you line up each precise shot while it charges, usually at long range.
mapping.reasoning: A linear fusion rifle charges before it fires, usually at range. You use the charge time to settle the reticle on the head. That is fine control at low aim speed for each deliberate shot, which is precision hold.
mapping.caveat: Based on how this weapon type fires, not on a source: no whitelisted source covers Destiny 2 weapons.

mapping.text: Rocket launchers are closest to precision-hold weapons: you line up one slow, explosive rocket at a time.
mapping.reasoning: A rocket launcher fires single slow projectiles with a big explosion, usually aimed at a target's feet or at a large target. Each shot is placed deliberately, and you are not holding on a target through sustained fire. That is closest to precision hold.
mapping.caveat: Based on how this weapon type fires, not on a source: no whitelisted source covers Destiny 2 weapons. Loose fit: splash damage makes exact aim matter less than with other weapons, and many rocket launchers also fire tracking rockets that lock onto targets when aimed (the Precision Frame, the Tracking Module perk, and exotics such as Truth), which makes it matter even less.
